articleTitle: IEE Colloquium on 'Computer Aided Acquisition and Logistics Support (CALS) - The UK Perspective' (Digest No.003)
publicationTitle: Computer Aided Acquisition and Logistics Support

articleTitle: Development of the CALS requirements and the status of its introduction and implementation in the United State and United States Air Force
publicationTitle: Computer Aided Acquisition and Logistics Support
abstract: The United States Air Force has long been a leader in the Department of Defense and Industry, through contractual relationships, for the implementation of new and innovative methods of doing business. The author discusses its implementation of computer-aided acquisition and logistics support (CALS). The CALS initiative was mandated by the Department of Defense (DoD) in 1985, to automate the way in which technical data will be procured, received, managed and used within the US armed services. The author considers its background, the CALS infrastructure, benefits, application and implementation philosophy.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The role of standard in CALS (computer-aided acquisition and logistics support)
publicationTitle: Computer Aided Acquisition and Logistics Support
abstract: CALS is an integrated environment for all data attributed to contract(s) from the birth of a product until its death. This will mean in the defence environment that the information will need to be accessible for tens of years. The types of data included will be: bids, specification, contractual, technology, implementation, test, manufacturing and procurement, etc. The author discusses the role of standards in CALS. CALS provides: consistent definitions of how information is transferred between the customer and the supplier; an environment where the maximum consensus can be achieved; a platform where investment decisions for the business infra-structure can be taken in the knowledge that changes to the technology will be made in an orderly fashion; and CALS products can be verified for suitability for inclusion in a users business.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Bidding experiences for CALS compliant projects (computer aided acquisition and logistics support)
publicationTitle: Computer Aided Acquisition and Logistics Support
abstract: Describes some experiences in bidding for a CALS contract including one approach which has been taken to the design of an infrastructure to support a CALS/CITIS requirement. Since the CITIS is, in essence, a new application software layer on a database management system the approach taken to the provision of a CITIS service has been that of applying open system techniques and partitioning the CALS problem 'in the large' into smaller problems and their interfaces. This approach has the major advantage that it eases the problems associated with multi-national operation. Further, changes in business policy during the bid process can be mapped into changes in the architecture at short notice.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The CALS Test Network verification and application testing strategy (military data management overview)
publicationTitle: Computer Aided Acquisition and Logistics Support
abstract: Discusses four major items in this paper: the CALS Test Network (GTN) objectives; user application testing and why it is important; general schedule for CALS testing and the strategy for services and industry to use in becoming CALS compatible; and benefits of the testing, to ones organization and to the Department of Defence. The CTN is composed of the Army, Navy, Air Force, and the Defense Logistics Agency, as well as numerous industry members and other US Government Agencies.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: Computer Aided Acquisition and Logistics Support
abstract: The title Concurrent (sometimes Simultaneous) engineering is used to bring together many techniques which have a single theme-the concurrent consideration of all constraints when making a design decision. The author discusses what makes up Concurrent Engineering. There are many methods of improving concept-to-market performance and most are included under the umbrella of Concurrent Engineering. He considers engineering design technology, creating teams and CE implementation.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Differences in the approach to the adoption of CALS in the United Kingdom and Europe to the United States
publicationTitle: Computer Aided Acquisition and Logistics Support
abstract: Discusses the policies on computer-aided acquisition and logistic support in the United Kingdom, Europe and the United States. The author considers areas such as special interest groups, standards, logistic support data and the way ahead.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: Computer Aided Acquisition and Logistics Support
abstract: The author covers the generalities of legal rights, especially how easy they are to generate and how easy they are to infringe. She comments mainly on UK law but with some references to other countries, especially if there are substantial differences. She discusses the six types of legal right protecting innovations, known as intellectual property rights. They are: copyright, registered design, design rights, patents, confidential information and trade marks. In the context of computer aided acquisition and logistic support she concentrates on copyright, design rights and confidential information.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
